1037.title: Punjab's drug crisis
1037.hook: families and gurdwaras are working to help young people out of addiction
1037.howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks Sikhs to avoid intoxicants. Some gurdwaras and Sikh organizations in Punjab and abroad support recovery work, youth programs and families facing addiction, alongside medical treatment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, caste, honestly, and your line was the gurus rejected it. Did you look at one bias of your own? Today, another hard subject, met the same way: with the lights on. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

A mother sits on the steps outside a gurdwara, holding her son's phone. He asked her to keep it. He's a few days into trying to stop, and he doesn't trust himself with the numbers saved inside it. Through the doors, kirtan is playing. A volunteer brings her a cup of tea and sits down next to her without asking a single question. In Punjab, families have been living stories like this one, and talking about them at kitchen tables, in songs, and in the gurdwara. Today isn't about blame. It's about the hands reaching in. Punjab's drug crisis.
screen: `A MOTHER HOLDS HER SON'S PHONE.` → `TEA, AND NO QUESTIONS.` → `THE HANDS REACHING IN.`

segments.voice: First, the hurt. Addiction in Punjab has reached into homes: a son, a cousin, a classmate, a neighbor's boy who used to play cricket in the lane. There are figures, and people argue about them. This lesson leaves them out, because behind every one of them is a person with a name. Second, what the Gurus said. In the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 554, Guru Amar Das describes what the false wine does: drinking it, a person loses their sense, can't tell their own from a stranger, and is pushed away from the Master. So, he says, don't drink this false wine at all, if it is in your power. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, carries the same teaching: Sikhs are asked to keep away from intoxicants, and the code names liquor, tobacco, opium and hemp among them. Third, the turn. The same salok doesn't stop at the warning. It speaks of a true wine, found by grace, by the one who meets the True Guru. The salok doesn't only take something away. It points to something to fill the empty place. Fourth, the hands. Families, doctors and sangats work on this together. Some gurdwaras and Sikh groups support recovery programs, sports for young people, and kirtan classes. Some sangats have learned to sit with a family instead of whispering about it. Shame keeps people hidden. A sangat that pulls a chair up to the table makes it easier to come out. That's today's line: help them out. Not lecture them out. Not shame them out. Help.
screen: `ADDICTION HAS REACHED INTO HOMES.` · `ANG 554: DON'T DRINK THE FALSE WINE.` · `A TRUE WINE, FOUND BY GRACE.` · `FAMILIES, DOCTORS AND SANGATS.` · then, large: `HELP THEM OUT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes on the steps. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Go back to the gurdwara steps from the story, and take the volunteer's place: a cup of tea in your hands, someone beside you who is carrying something heavy. It might be the mother. It might be someone you know, struggling with a drink, a drug, a screen, grief, or something they haven't told anyone. Don't speak. Don't fix anything. Just stay. Breathe in, and feel the warmth of the cup. Breathe out, and keep your place on the step. Sitting there is the whole job. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Punjab's drug crisis. The addiction that has reached into Punjabi homes, and the families, gurdwaras and doctors working to bring young people out of it. Today's word.

Your line: help them out. Today, offer one struggling person one small kindness, without a lecture attached. And if someone is in danger, get them to a doctor or emergency help first. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

1038.title: Choosing the turban
1038.hook: young Sikhs decide for themselves how to keep kesh and turban
1038.howItsDone: Sikhs who take amrit keep kesh, uncut hair, as one of the five articles of faith, and Sikh men and some Sikh women cover it with a turban. Some young Sikhs begin with a patka and decide for themselves when to tie a full turban.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's drug crisis, and your line was help them out. Did you offer one kindness without a lecture attached? Today, young Sikhs again, and a choice that's theirs to make. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

Sunday morning. A teenager stands at the bathroom mirror with a long strip of cloth over one shoulder and a phone propped against the tap, playing a tying tutorial at half speed. Fold, wrap, pin, start again. Down the hall, a younger brother still wears a patka, the small cloth their mother ties for him each morning. The teenager could have kept the patka. Could have stopped covering at all. Instead, this morning, the cloth goes round once more, and it holds. Today, how young Sikhs decide for themselves. Choosing the turban.
screen: `A STRIP OF CLOTH AND A TUTORIAL.` → `FOLD, WRAP, PIN, AGAIN.` → `THIS MORNING, IT HOLDS.`

segments.voice: First, what's being kept. Kesh, uncut hair, is one of the five articles of faith. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, asks Sikhs who have taken amrit to keep their hair uncut, and the turban covers and honors it. Second, the choosing. Young Sikhs come to this in different ways. Some grow up in a patka and move to a full turban. Some girls choose a turban, or a keski, a smaller one. Some cut their hair for years and later decide to grow it back. Families argue about it, and pray about it, and still sit down to dinner. The gurdwara door stays open to all of them. Third, why choice matters. Tradition remembers the day Guru Gobind Singh called the Khalsa into being: he asked who would come forward, and one by one, five did. And the Rehat Maryada asks that those who take amrit be old enough to understand what they're promising. The Khalsa begins with a person stepping forward. Fourth, what the choice looks like now. It can mean a tutorial at half speed. It can mean wearing a turban to a new school, or into a job interview, or onto a sports field, and answering the same question politely, again and again. It can mean waiting until you're sure. That's today's line: their choice. Some Sikhs put it this way: a turban tied because you chose it becomes a promise you keep.

segments.voice: Two minutes for someone else's choice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one person who chose something you might not have chosen: what they wear, what they believe, what they gave up, what they took on. Breathe in, and picture them making that decision, maybe at a mirror, maybe late at night. Breathe out, and let go of the urge to vote on it. It's theirs. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Choosing the turban. Young Sikhs deciding for themselves how to keep their uncut hair and whether and how to tie a turban, a choice the tradition wants made with understanding. Today's word.
Your line: their choice. Today, when someone tells you about a decision they made about faith or identity, ask one question to understand it, and offer no verdict. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

1039.title: Gurmukhi on screens
1039.hook: the Granth is now searchable online, with translations
1039.howItsDone: Sikhs use websites and apps to search the Guru Granth Sahib by ang or by the first letters of a line, and some gurdwaras project the hymn being sung in Gurmukhi with a transliteration and a translation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, choosing the turban, and your line was their choice. Did you ask one question and hold back the verdict? Today, the tutorial on the phone gets a bigger job: carrying the Guru's word. Day one thousand thirty-nine.

At the back of a gurdwara, a girl leans toward her grandfather and whispers, what's that line? The ragis are singing, and she can't quite catch it. He doesn't open a book. He points at the wall. A screen there shows the line in Gurmukhi, then the same sounds in Roman letters underneath, then a meaning in English. She reads along, mouthing the words. Her grandfather reads the top line. She reads the bottom two. For a moment they're singing the same hymn from different ends of the screen. Today, Gurmukhi on screens.
screen: `WHAT'S THAT LINE?` → `GURMUKHI, SOUNDS, MEANING.` → `ONE HYMN, TWO ENDS OF A SCREEN.`

segments.voice: First, the page. The Guru Granth Sahib is read by ang, the word Sikhs use for its pages. Printed copies keep the same page layout, which is why these lessons can send you to one ang and you'll find the same hymn there. Second, the screen. Today the whole Granth can be searched on a phone or a website. Some tools let you type just the first letter of each word, so a half-remembered line can still be found. In some gurdwaras, the line being sung goes up on a screen with a transliteration and a translation, so someone who can't read Gurmukhi can follow along. Third, a careful step. Sikhs treat the Gurmukhi as the Guru's own word. A translation underneath is a helper: one person's reading, made with care, but not the Guru. Different translations sometimes disagree, and that's a reason to go back to the top line, not away from it. Fourth, the root. At Ang 982, Guru Ram Das says it plainly: bani guru, guru hai bani. The Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word, and within the Word is all the nectar. For Sikhs who hold that, a screen that carries the Word into the back row can be a kind of seva: a lamp moved closer to the people who couldn't see. That's today's line: the word online. Not a replacement for the Granth. A way to reach it.
screen: `READ BY ANG, THE SAME PAGES.` · `SEARCH BY FIRST LETTERS.` · `A TRANSLATION IS A HELPER.` · `BANI GURU, GURU HAI BANI.` · then, large: `THE WORD ONLINE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with one line. Sit, and let the breath slow. If you have a screen nearby, you can open any ang of the Guru Granth Sahib and pick one line. If not, use today's: bani guru, guru hai bani. Read it, or say it, slowly. Then sit with what it means: the Word is the Guru. Breathe in with the first half. Breathe out with the second. Don't hurry to the next line. One is enough. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end. The bell holds the time.
Gurmukhi on screens. The Guru Granth Sahib searchable online and shown in gurdwaras with transliteration and translation, so more people can reach the Word itself. Today's word.
Your line: the word online. Today, look up one ang, read its Gurmukhi line once even if you only sound out the letters, and then read a translation underneath. Day one thousand thirty-nine.

1040.title: The old strings return
1040.hook: musicians are reviving the rebab, saranda and taus for kirtan
1040.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, kirtan is usually sung with harmonium and tabla. Some Sikh musicians and teachers now also teach and perform kirtan on string instruments such as the rabab, saranda, taus and dilruba, in the raags the hymns are set in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurmukhi on screens, and your line was the word online. Did you look up one ang? Today the newest tool steps back, and some of the oldest come forward. Day one thousand forty.

A wooden case clicks open on a classroom floor. Inside is an instrument shaped a little like a lute, with a skin-covered belly and a short neck. A teacher lifts it out the way you'd lift a sleeping baby, tunes it slowly, and plucks one string. The note is low and dry, and it hangs in the air a long time. A row of students with harmoniums on their laps goes quiet. Some of them have never heard one played in person. This sound, Sikh tradition says, was there at the very start of kirtan. Today, the old strings return.
screen: `A WOODEN CASE CLICKS OPEN.` → `ONE LOW, DRY NOTE.` → `THERE AT THE START.`

segments.voice: First, the rabab. Sikh tradition remembers Bhai Mardana, Guru Nanak's companion on his long journeys, playing the rabab while the Guru sang. Guru Nanak's hymns were first heard, tradition says, over strings like these. Second, the other strings. Tradition links the saranda, a bowed instrument, to Guru Arjan, and the taus, a bowed instrument carved in the shape of a peacock, to Guru Hargobind. Each carries a Guru's name in the tradition's memory. Third, the quiet and the return. Over time, the harmonium, a later arrival, became the familiar sound of kirtan in gurdwaras. It's easy to carry and easy to learn, and it carries hymns beautifully. But the old strings grew rare. Now musicians and teachers are bringing them back: building rababs and tauses again, teaching the raags the hymns are set in, and playing kirtan the older way. Some sangats welcome it. Some love the harmonium they grew up with. Both are kirtan. Fourth, the root. In Raag Asa, at Ang 350, Guru Nanak names the instrument underneath every instrument: let understanding be your instrument, and love your drum. Then bliss comes, and the mind is always eager. A string can be revived. A raag can be relearned. But what makes it kirtan is the listening heart behind it. That's today's line: old strings return. Not to replace anything. To remind everyone where the song began.
screen: `BHAI MARDANA'S RABAB.` · `SARANDA AND TAUS.` · `THE HARMONIUM, AND THE REVIVAL.` · `UNDERSTANDING THE INSTRUMENT, LOVE THE DRUM.` · then, large: `OLD STRINGS RETURN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of listening. If you can, play a recording of kirtan on a string instrument, softly. If not, just listen to the room: the hum of a fridge, traffic, a bird, your own breath. Sit, and don't name the sounds. Let them arrive and fade, the way a plucked string fades. Breathe in as a sound begins. Breathe out as it ends. Notice the space between notes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The old strings return. Musicians reviving the rabab, the saranda and the taus, instruments tradition links to the Gurus, so kirtan can be heard again the older way. Today's word.
Your line: old strings return. Today, listen to one piece of music played on a string instrument, all the way through, without doing anything else. Day one thousand forty.

1041.title: Cleaning a river
1041.hook: volunteers cleaned the Kali Bein, the river where Nanak disappeared, by kar seva
1041.howItsDone: Kar seva is volunteer labor for a sacred place, such as cleaning a gurdwara's sarovar or building and repairing gurdwaras. At Sultanpur Lodhi, volunteers have cleaned the Kali Bein by kar seva, and Sikhs visit the Gurdwara Ber Sahib there, linked with the story of Guru Nanak's disappearance in the river.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the old strings return, and your line was old strings return. Did you listen to one piece all the way through? Today, something else old comes back to life, and this time it's a river. Day one thousand forty-one.

Mud up to the knees. A line of volunteers stands in a narrow, choked stream, passing buckets of black silt and tangled weeds from hand to hand up the bank. Some are farmers. Some are students. Some came after work. Nobody is paid. The water barely moves, and it smells. But the stories of Guru Nanak know the name of this stream. It's the Kali Bein, at Sultanpur Lodhi, the river where, the stories say, Nanak went into the water and vanished. Today, cleaning a river.
screen: `MUD TO THE KNEES.` → `BUCKETS UP THE BANK.` → `THE KALI BEIN.`

segments.voice: First, the river in the story. The janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak, tell of the morning he went to bathe in the Bein and vanished. Tradition says he was gone for three days, and that when he came back, his first words were: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. This path told that story long ago. Today, the river itself. Second, what happened to the river. In our own times the Kali Bein was choked with weeds and waste, and dirty water ran into it. The river of that story was hard to recognize. Third, the hands. Volunteers began to clean it by kar seva, the Sikh name for free, hands-on work for a sacred place, the same kind of work that has cleaned the pools at gurdwaras. A Sikh sant, Balbir Singh Seechewal, is known for leading it. They cleared weeds and silt by hand, worked on stopping the dirty water, and planted the banks. Over time, the water ran again. Fourth, the root. In the Asa di Var, at Ang 472, Guru Nanak says that first of all, water is life, by which everything is made green. If water is where life begins, then a dirty river isn't only an eyesore. It's a wound in the place the Guru called life itself. So the volunteers didn't treat it as a project. They treated it as seva. That's today's line: clean the river. The Guru disappeared into that water. They made sure there was water worth coming back out of.
screen: `NANAK VANISHED INTO THE BEIN.` · `THE RIVER CHOKED WITH WASTE.` · `KAR SEVA, BUCKET BY BUCKET.` · `FIRST, WATER IS LIFE.` · then, large: `CLEAN THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with water. Sit, and if you can, set a glass of water in front of you. Look at it. Breathe in, and think of where it came from: a river, a reservoir, rain on a hillside far away. Breathe out, and think of where it goes when you're done with it. Somewhere downstream, someone else drinks it, or a field, or a fish. Let the breath be slow and plain. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. Then take one sip, and notice it. The bell holds the time.
Cleaning a river. Volunteers clearing the Kali Bein by kar seva, the river where tradition says Guru Nanak disappeared and came back with his first teaching. Today's word.

Your line: clean the river. Today, pick up litter near water: a creek, a drain, a beach, a fountain, even a gutter that runs to a stream. Do it safely, with gloves or a bag. Day one thousand forty-one.

1042.title: Planting forests
1042.hook: Sikh groups plant small forests to honor Guru Nanak
1042.howItsDone: Some Sikh organizations and sangats plant small, dense forests of native trees near gurdwaras, schools and villages in honor of Guru Nanak, and Sikhs recite the Japji's closing salok, which names air, water and earth as Guru, father and mother.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cleaning a river, and your line was clean the river. Did you pick up something near water? Today the volunteers climb out of the river and pick up shovels. Day one thousand forty-two.

A scrap of land behind a village school. Hard dirt, a broken wall, a pile of bricks nobody moved. A sangat arrives after the Sunday program with saplings in plastic bags, a cart of compost, and a list of trees that belong to this soil. They don't plant in neat rows with space between. They plant close, shoulder to shoulder, the way a real forest grows. Children help press the earth down around each stem. A few seasons later, that scrap of dirt is a green wall full of birds. It was planted for one person. Today, planting forests.
screen: `A SCRAP OF HARD DIRT.` → `SAPLINGS SHOULDER TO SHOULDER.` → `A GREEN WALL OF BIRDS.`

segments.voice: First, the idea. Sikh groups have been planting small, dense forests in honor of Guru Nanak, on patches of land near gurdwaras, schools, farms and villages. Some call them Guru Nanak sacred forests. Second, the method. Instead of a few big trees far apart, they plant native trees and shrubs close together, so they compete for light and grow fast and thick. Some groups use a way of planting that comes from Japan. The point is a real forest on a small plot, not a park. Third, the root. Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning end it with a short salok, at Ang 8. In Gurmukhi it begins: pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat. Air is the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother. So a forest isn't decoration. It's a family: air, water and earth, the ones the Guru named as teacher and parents. Fourth, the old green thread. Tradition remembers Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, keeping gardens and growing healing herbs, and tells of him as a boy brushing a flower with his robe and breaking it, and taking care with every living thing after that. The forests carry that thread forward. A tree planted for Nanak gives shade to anyone, of any faith, who sits under it. That's today's line: a forest for nanak. It honors the Guru by giving the earth, the great mother of the salok, back a little of what was taken.
screen: `SMALL FORESTS FOR GURU NANAK.` · `NATIVE TREES, PLANTED CLOSE.` · `AIR GURU, WATER FATHER, EARTH MOTHER.` · `GURU HAR RAI'S GARDENS.` · then, large: `A FOREST FOR NANAK.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the three the Guru named. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Breathe in, and notice the air: the Guru, the salok says. Feel your feet on the floor, and below the floor the earth: the great mother. Think of the water inside you, in every cell: the father. Air, water, earth. Stay with whichever one is easiest to feel. If you pray, you can say pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat once, slowly. The bell holds the time.
Planting forests. Sikh groups planting small, dense forests of native trees to honor Guru Nanak, who named air as Guru, water as father and earth as the great mother. Today's word.
Your line: a forest for nanak. Today, plant or water something: a seed in a pot, a houseplant that's been ignored, a street tree in a dry week. Day one thousand forty-two.

1043.title: The kitchen at Amritsar
1043.hook: the langar at the Golden Temple feeds tens of thousands every day
1043.howItsDone: At the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the langar serves free vegetarian meals to all visitors, who sit together in rows (pangat) on the floor; volunteers cook, serve and wash the dishes as seva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, planting forests, and your line was a forest for nanak. Did you plant or water something? Today, from the forest to a kitchen in Amritsar. Day one thousand forty-three.

The sound comes first. Steel plates, stacked and passed and clattering, a rolling metal river of them. Then the smell: lentils, butter, fresh roti. Then the hall itself, at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, also called the Golden Temple. People sit on long strips of matting on the floor, row after row: a farmer, a tourist with a camera around her neck, a businessman, a grandmother, a child. A volunteer walks down the row with a bucket of dal, ladling it onto every plate in the same amount. Nobody asks who you are. Today, the kitchen at Amritsar.
screen: `A RIVER OF STEEL PLATES.` → `ROW AFTER ROW ON THE FLOOR.` → `NOBODY ASKS WHO YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: First, the size. The gurdwara's own accounts say its langar feeds tens of thousands of people every day, and more on festival days. The food is free. Volunteers do much of the work: kneading dough, rolling roti, stirring huge pots, washing plates. Second, the rows. The sitting in rows is called pangat. Everyone eats at the same level, the same food, from the same kitchen. There is no head table, and no better plate for an important guest. Third, the emperor on the floor. Tradition tells that when the emperor Akbar came to meet Guru Amar Das, he was asked to do what everyone did first: sit in the pangat and eat langar. Sikhs sum up the old rule in a short phrase: pehle pangat, piche sangat. First the row, then the gathering. A ruler of an empire, the story goes, sat on the floor beside whoever was there. Fourth, the plates. After the meal comes the washing. Visitors line up to scrub steel next to students and farmers. The hands get wrinkled, the plates go back out, and the river keeps flowing. That's today's line: tens of thousands fed. Not a statistic. A meal, multiplied, and every plate given the same.
screen: `FREE FOOD, CARRIED BY VOLUNTEERS.` · `PANGAT: EVERYONE IN THE SAME ROW.` · `FIRST THE ROW, THEN THE GATHERING.` · `WASHING THE PLATES.` · then, large: `TENS OF THOUSANDS FED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in the rows. Sit, and let your breath slow. Picture the hall: the long mats, the people sitting side by side, the volunteer coming down the line with a bucket. Put yourself in the row. Who's on your left? A stranger. On your right? Another. Now see the plate land in front of you, the same as theirs. Breathe in, receiving. Breathe out, and picture yourself up at the sinks, washing someone else's plate. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The kitchen at Amritsar. The langar of the Harmandir Sahib, where volunteers cook and serve free meals to everyone who comes, all seated together in rows. Today's word.

Your line: tens of thousands fed. That ends a week of Sikh life now: help out of addiction, a turban chosen, the word on screens, old strings, a clean river, a forest, and this kitchen. Today, at one meal, serve someone else first, or wash a plate that isn't yours. Day one thousand forty-three.
